name: Daptomycin
evidenceNote: Daptomycin has been FDA-approved since 2003, based on two randomized skin infection trials with over 1,000 patients and a later randomized trial in Staph aureus bloodstream infection.
summary: An IV antibiotic for serious skin and bloodstream infections, including MRSA. FDA-approved since 2003; not used for pneumonia because lung fluid inactivates it.
keyTakeaway: Daptomycin is a hospital antibiotic given by IV once a day to treat complicated skin infections, as well as bloodstream infections with Staphylococcus aureus, right-sided heart valve infection included. It was the first approved drug in its class, the cyclic lipopeptides, and kills gram-positive bacteria such as MRSA by collapsing the electrical charge across their membranes. In a randomized trial of bloodstream infection it matched standard therapy, with 44% versus 42% success, and caused less kidney injury. It does not work for pneumonia, and muscle damage is the side effect doctors watch most closely.

blocks.text: Daptomycin is an antibiotic made from a compound produced by the soil bacterium Streptomyces roseosporus [1][6]. Chemically it is a cyclic lipopeptide, a ring of amino acids with a fatty tail attached, and it was the first drug of that class to reach patients [4]. It is given only into a vein.

It is used for serious infections caused by gram-positive bacteria, including strains that resist older drugs, such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) [4][6]. Doctors also use it, outside the label, for vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) [6]. It was sold first as Cubicin and is now made by many generic manufacturers [2][7].

Daptomycin attaches to the outer membrane of bacterial cells and causes a rapid loss of the electrical charge across it, called depolarization [1]. Bacteria depend on that charge to run their machinery, so once it collapses they stop making DNA, RNA, and proteins and die [1]. Because it kills bacteria directly rather than only halting their growth, it is described as bactericidal.

That membrane-seeking behavior also explains its main blind spot. In the lungs, daptomycin binds to surfactant, the fatty film that lines the air sacs, and loses its activity there [5]. A clinical trial in severe community-acquired pneumonia failed to show it was as good as comparison drugs, which is why the label excludes pneumonia [5][1]. How bacteria become resistant is not fully understood, and no transferable resistance genes are known [1].

In healthy adults the drug has a half-life of about eight hours and leaves the body mostly through the kidneys, so people with poor kidney function receive doses spaced 48 hours apart instead of 24 [1].

Yes. The FDA first approved daptomycin, as Cubicin, on September 12, 2003, as a new molecular entity under priority review [2]. Its indications later grew to include Staph aureus bloodstream infections and use in children aged 1 to 17 [1][3].

The original Cubicin vials are listed as discontinued in the FDA's drug database [2], but daptomycin itself remains widely available: dozens of generic labels from manufacturers such as Fresenius Kabi, Camber, and NorthStar are listed on DailyMed [7]. A reformulated Cubicin RF label remains current [1].

items: Complicated skin and skin structure infections in adults and in children aged 1 to 17 [1].
Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infections (bacteremia) in adults, including right-sided infective endocarditis, and in children aged 1 to 17 [1].
Not indicated for pneumonia or for left-sided endocarditis, and not recommended for children under 1 year [1].

blocks.text: Two randomized international trials compared it with standard antibiotics in 1,092 patients with complicated skin infections. Clinical success was 83.4% with daptomycin and 84.2% with the comparators, and most patients who did well on daptomycin needed only four to seven days of IV treatment [4].

rows: 246 patients with Staph aureus bacteremia or endocarditis
Kidney dysfunction 11.0% vs 26.3% with standard therapy [3]

blocks.text: The bloodstream trial is the reason for the second indication. Daptomycin was as effective as low-dose gentamicin plus an anti-staph penicillin or vancomycin, including in MRSA and right-sided endocarditis [3]. It caused less kidney damage, but microbiologic failure was more common (19 vs 11 patients), and in six of those daptomycin patients the bacteria became less susceptible to the drug [3].

Muscle injury is the signature risk. Daptomycin can cause myopathy and, rarely, rhabdomyolysis (rapid muscle breakdown), so the label calls for monitoring of CPK, a blood marker of muscle damage, and stopping the drug if it rises sharply with symptoms [1]. Other warnings include eosinophilic pneumonia, a lung reaction driven by a type of white blood cell; severe skin and organ reactions such as DRESS; kidney inflammation; nerve damage; and C. difficile diarrhea [1].

Common, milder effects in adults with skin infections included diarrhea, headache, dizziness, rash, abnormal liver tests, and raised CPK [1]. In children, vomiting, abdominal pain, itching, and fever were also reported [1]. Some laboratory clotting tests can read falsely high while a person is on daptomycin [1].

Kidney function also shapes how well it works. In the bacteremia trial, adults with moderately reduced kidney function (creatinine clearance below 50 mL/min) had lower success rates on daptomycin, a finding the label lists among its warnings [1].
